theme.name: Productivity gap
theme.claim: Despite considerable economic strengths, Midlands productivity has fallen further behind the UK average (gap widening from about 10% to 15% between 1997 and 2015), with GVA per employee and business creation lagging.

text.line: Its economy is worth £217.7 billion - 13% of the UK’s annual output.

It has the UK’s second largest city – Birmingham – which is already growing rapidly: in 2014/2015, Birmingham’s economy grew by 5.1%. 1. Over the next few years, there are major opportunities to build on this base. ** (Reference: 3)
1.5 Over and above its well-known manufacturing strengths, the Midlands Engine economy has a strong services base.
In 2015 Gross Value Added (GVA) in the service sector was £158.4 billion, 72.8% of total GVA in East and West Midlands. ** (Reference: 5)

The Midlands Engine Science and Innovation Audit highlighted that in 2014 the Midlands Engine accounted for 14% of UK GVA in real estate activity, 13% in business services and 9% in financial and insurance activities. ** (Reference: 6,7)
However, despite these strengths, the Midlands economy has been falling behind over recent years.

In 1997, the productivity gap between the Midlands and the UK average was about 10%. By 2015, it had grown to about 15%. This productivity challenge applies across both rural and urban areas. ** (Reference: 8,9)
4.4 However, despite these strengths, productivity in the Midlands still lags behind the national average.
GVA per employee in the Midlands is £44,447 compared to the UK

average of £50,830. This is true even in areas of comparative strength – GVA per employee in manufacturing in the Midlands is 23.90% below the UK average. 4. This is reflected in the lack of dynamism in the Midlands’ economy. ** (Reference: 5,41,42)
Despite the area’s research strengths, in 2015, there were 54 new companies created per 10,000 people in the East Midlands, and just 51 in the West Midlands.
This is about 25% below the England average of 70, and less than half of the figure for London. ** (Reference: 43)

theme.name: Skills shortage
theme.claim: The Midlands has a weaker skills base than other regions, with fewer highly qualified people, more with no qualifications, weaker school outcomes and poor graduate retention, which explains regional disparities in growth and productivity.

text.line: The Midlands economy suffers from three key weaknesses that we need to address.
First, there is a shortage of skilled workers.

The proportion of highly skilled people is about 15% below the England average. One in every eight people in the West Midlands has no qualifications. And too many skilled graduates are leaving the region after completing their studies. ** (Reference: 10,11)
This makes it more expensive for people, goods and ideas to move around, holding back innovation and making it harder for people to find jobs that match their skills.
Ultimately, this lowers productivity, and wages.
Opportunities and Challenges 3. Regional disparities in skills are crucial to explaining regional disparities in growth and productivity. ** (Reference: 1)
Businesses will choose to locate and expand in places where they can easily find people with the skills they need.

This was about 14% higher than the England average of 920. 3. However, these strengths should not obscure the underlying story: the Midlands skills base is weak compared to other regions. ** (Reference: 5,23)
Across England, 36.8% of people have at least a qualification that is equivalent to a degree and this rises to nearly 50% in London. ** (Reference: 24)
The figures for the East and West Midlands are 31.8% and 31.2% respectively. ** (Reference: 25)
The West Midlands is the region with the highest proportion of people with no qualifications – 13%. ** (Reference: 26)

The inactivity rate in the West Midlands is 23.1%, compared to the national average of 21.6%. As a result, in 2015, at least 30,000 vacancies were hard to fill because of a lack of suitably skilled candidates. 3. ** (Reference: 6,27,28,29)
This situation reflects two facts: first, outcomes in schools in the Midlands are below the national average.
More than a quarter of secondary schools in the Midlands are not reaching the required standards set out by Ofsted. ** (Reference: 30)
The West Midlands is the joint worst performing region, along with Yorkshire and the Humber, for primary school outcomes. ** (Reference: 31)
3.7 Second, the Midlands struggles to retain the graduates it educates, and also to attract graduates from other parts of the country.

Just 37.9% of graduates in the East Midlands who are in work six months after graduation, are working in the region. The figure for the West Midlands is 55.4%. In contrast, London retains 69.2% of its graduates. ** (Reference: 32,33,34)

theme.name: Fragmented transport and connectivity
theme.claim: Slow, congested transport links within the region and a dispersed population fragment the economy, raising the cost of moving people, goods and ideas and lowering productivity and wages, despite good national and international links.

text.line: 1.9 Second, the region’s economy is fragmented into small, poorly connected areas.
This means that the whole sometimes adds up to less than the sum of its parts and the Midlands isn’t making the most of its position at the centre of the country.
However, transport connections within the region are often too slow and congested.

There were over six million hours of delays across the Midlands Motorway Hub in 2014/2015. It takes nearly three hours to travel just over 100 miles from Leicester in the North East of the region to Hereford in the South West by train - more than three times as long as it will take to travel a similar distance from London to Birmingham once HS2 opens. ** (Reference: 20)
The weakness of transport connections within the region is a particular problem because of the dispersed nature of the population.
Even though Birmingham is the second largest city in the UK, the Midlands’ population is considerably more spread out than most other regions of England.
This makes it more expensive for people, goods and ideas to move around, holding back innovation and making it harder for people to find jobs that match their skills.
Ultimately, this lowers productivity, and wages.

references.reference: Midlands Connect (2016). Picking up the Pace – pg 14

theme.name: Existing strengths to build on
theme.claim: The region has substantial assets (large economy, manufacturing and services base, industrial clusters, 20 universities, strong exports and inward investment) that provide a base for growth if the weaknesses are addressed.

text.line: It is already home to more than ten million people.
Its economy is worth £217.7 billion - 13% of the UK’s annual output.

It has the UK’s second largest city – Birmingham – which is already growing rapidly: in 2014/2015, Birmingham’s economy grew by 5.1%. 1. Over the next few years, there are major opportunities to build on this base. ** (Reference: 3)
This region is already the headquarters for a range of globally significant businesses, including Jaguar Land Rover, JCB and Rolls Royce.
Last year, the Midlands accounted

for 19.1% of all English goods exports going to over 100 countries. It is home to a number of nationally significant clusters, including advanced manufacturing in the Black Country and Derbyshire, the automotive cluster around Coventry and Warwickshire, and the ceramics industry in Stoke and Staffordshire. ** (Reference: 4)
The Midlands’ science and research base is also strong: the region has 20 universities, with research strengths ranging from civil engineering to space technology.
First, the Midlands’ geographical location at the centre of the UK gives it an inherent advantage in ensuring it is well connected to the wider UK economy.
92% of the UK’s population can reach the Midlands in less than four hours. 45% of British rail freight goes through the Midlands. ** (Reference: 13,14)
2.3 Second, the Midlands is already quite well connected to the international economy.
Birmingham Airport handles more than ten million passengers each year. East Midlands airport is the second largest freight airport in the country. ** (Reference: 15,16)
2.4 Third, the Midlands has comparatively strong digital infrastructure.

The UK average for superfast broadband coverage is 92.4%. In the East Midlands, 95.2% of households can access superfast broadband. In the West Midlands, the figure is 94.7%. 2. ** (Reference: 5,17,18,19)
The Midlands has key strengths on which we can build.
First, the Midlands is home to 20 universities.
These include three universities that have been ranked in the top 150 in the world – Warwick, Birmingham, and Nottingham.
The thriving higher education sector in the region provides a valuable base for ensuring the region has the skills it
needs to attract businesses.
Second, the Midlands has a bedrock of highly skilled, specialist employees in high value manufacturing.
Over 600,000 people in the Midlands work in manufacturing, delivering over 21% of the UK’s annual manufacturing output. ** (Reference: 21)
3.4 Third, the Midlands has a strong tradition of apprenticeships, reflecting its industrial heritage.
In 2015/2016, there were 1,045 apprenticeship starts per 100,000 people in the Midlands. ** (Reference: 22)
Challenges and Opportunities 4. The Midlands is home to a range of nationally significant clusters of industry and expertise. ** (Reference: 1)
This was highlighted by the recent Midlands Engine Science and Innovation Audit.
The area’s sectoral strengths include:
 Advanced manufacturing, particularly in the Black Country and Derbyshire.
The Midlands accounts for over 21% of UK manufacturing output.  ** (Reference: 35)
Automotive cluster in Coventry and Warwickshire, where several

internationally renowned companies are based, including Jaguar Land Rover, BMW, General Electric, and Aston Martin Lagonda. 39% of employment in the UK automotive sector is located in the Midlands.  ** (Reference: 36)
Connected and Autonomous vehicles, much of the UK’s world-leading
capabilities in this emerging sector is located in the Midlands, ranging from the UK Autodrive driverless car trial jointly run by Coventry and Milton
Keynes, the Transport Systems Catapult, the Nissan Technical Centre Europe (Cranfield), and leading proving grounds like Millbrook and Horiba Mira.
 Ceramics in Stoke and Staffordshire.
The ceramics industry employs 4,800

people in the West Midlands; this is over double the number of people employed in all the other UK regions combined.  Life sciences and medical devices in Birmingham and Nottingham. ** (Reference: 37)
The
Midlands has more medical technology companies than any other region of the UK.  Agri-food and drink processing, particularly in Lincolnshire, the Marches ** (Reference: 38)
and Leicestershire.
132,000 people in the Midlands work in this sector, across 33,000 companies.  Space technology around the Space Research Centre and Earth ** (Reference: 39)
Observation Centre in Leicester.
 Digital technology, including in the cyber security clusters in Malvern and
Nottingham, and the games development clusters in Leamington Spa and Coventry.
Approximately 139,000 people are employed in the digital technology economy in the Midlands. 4. These clusters are underpinned by the region’s strong science and research base. ** (Reference: 2,40)
The Midlands’ 20 universities have research strengths across a range of areas, including manufacturing technology, civil engineering, and space technology.
Six research intensive universities in the Midlands have come together to form Midlands Innovation, a world-class university research and innovation partnership.

From the National Automotive Innovation Centre at the University of Warwick to the Life Sciences Campus in Birmingham, and from the space research in Leicester to the Carbon Neutral Laboratory for Sustainable Chemistry, a collaboration between the University of Nottingham and GlaxoSmithKline, the Midlands is home to world leading research across a range of specialisms.
The region has key assets including the National Exhibition Centre and International Convention Centre in Birmingham, hosting national and internationally focused conferences and events.
IBM’s Client Innovation Centre is in Leicester, providing high value application development and maintenance and systems management services.
And the Midlands Engine is home to a number of notable clusters of innovative firms - from cyber security in Malvern and Nottingham, to the games development clusters in Leamington Spa and Coventry.
Challenges and Opportunities 5. The Midlands has strong connections to the rest of the world. ** (Reference: 1)

The region has two international airports, serving over 14.6 million passengers a year, and flying to over 200 countries. It also has some of the best shipping ports in the UK, in Greater Lincolnshire. ** (Reference: 44,45)
The Ports of Grimsby and Immingham combined form the UK’s largest port by tonnage, handling 59.1 million tonnes of cargo each year. 5. ** (Reference: 2,46)
The region is an attractive place for investors.

It is well connected to other areas of the UK: 92% of the UK’s population is within a four hour commute of the Midlands. 31% of the population is under 25, offering a young, dynamic pool of labour for businesses. ** (Reference: 47,48)
Reflecting these advantages, the Midlands has performed well on inward investment over recent years.

Since 2011, over 1,000 projects have secured foreign investment in the region, creating or safeguarding over 100,000 jobs. Foreign investors have helped to catalyse growth in the region, through acting as anchors for local economies, and supporting extensive supply chains across the region. ** (Reference: 49)
5.4 Midlands exports have also performed strongly.

In 2015, the Midlands region exported £39.9bn worth of products to over 100 countries. This represented an increase of 6.5% from 2014 – the largest rise in exports of any UK region. ** (Reference: 50,51)
Challenges and Opportunities 6. Successful places need to be able to attract dynamic, skilled workers who can drive local productivity and growth. ** (Reference: 1)
The Midlands encompasses some of the most renowned natural, historical and cultural sites in the country.
From the UNESCO
World Heritage sites of Derwent Valley Mills and Ironbridge Gorge, to the Peak District National Park and the National Forest, the Midlands has a rich cultural and natural heritage.

Reflecting this in 2015, 20.1 million overseas and domestic overnight visits were made to the Midlands, with inbound visits alone contributing £1.25 billion spend. This is in addition to over 230 million day visits. In 2013, the economic value (GVA) of tourism in the Midlands was £6.33 billion. 6. Increasing housing supply is central to the government’s vision of a country that works for everyone. ** (Reference: 3,52,53,54,55,56)
However, across the Midlands there is a need to provide even more housing for future generations.

text.line: Modernising digital infrastructure 2. Digital connectivity is also crucial to raising productivity and living standards. ** (Reference: 17)
The internet has revolutionised the way we work.
Superfast broadband is already supporting economic growth, raising business productivity, and improving quality of life for residents.
We need to ensure that the Midlands’ digital infrastructure keeps pace with national and international competitors.
